title: A small fish
hook: govern a great country as you'd cook a small fish, without too much poking (Tao Te Ching 60)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was frugal living, from chapter fifty-nine: what isn't wasted becomes a reserve. Your line was frugal.

A small fish is sizzling in a pan. Someone stands over it with a spatula and can't leave it alone. Lift the edge, check the color, nudge it, flip it, flip it back. By the time it's cooked, it's in flakes all over the pan, and there isn't much fish left to serve. Chapter sixty of the Tao Te Ching sets that kitchen scene right next to a far bigger job: running a country. It sounds like a joke. It isn't.
screen: `A FISH IN A HOT PAN.` → `FLIP, CHECK, FLIP AGAIN.` → `A COUNTRY IN THE SAME PAN.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In James Legge's translation, chapter sixty opens: "Governing a great state is like cooking small fish." That's the whole instruction; it leaves the cook to work out the how. Second, why a small fish. A thick cut of meat can take some handling, but a small fish is delicate. An old commentary, the one tradition credits to Heshang Gong, reads it this way: don't dare to stir it, or it falls apart. So the skill is mostly restraint: get the heat right, put it in, let it cook. A country, in this picture, is fragile in the same way, and every new order, every shake-up, every fresh rule turns the fish over once more. Third, the stranger second half. When the world is ruled by the Tao, the chapter says, the spirits of the dead lose their power to harm. Not that they have no power, it adds, but that it doesn't hurt people. And the sage doesn't hurt people either. When neither side does harm, their goodness flows together. Some readers hear old beliefs about ghosts; some hear that a calm, unmeddling order leaves less room for dread of any kind. The text doesn't settle it. Fourth, the small fish in daily life: an inbox, a team, a teenager's homework, a sourdough starter, a friendship that went quiet. The pull is to keep turning it: one more text, one more check, one more tweak to the plan. Chapter sixty leaves a plain kitchen question on the counter. Is this still cooking, or is it just poking?
screen: `A GREAT STATE, A SMALL FISH.` · `EVERY TURN BREAKS IT A LITTLE.` · `SPIRITS THAT DO NO HARM.` · then, large: `COOKING, OR JUST POKING?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been turning over and over: a message you keep rereading, a plan you keep adjusting, a person you keep checking on. For these two minutes, set the spatula down; the fish is in the pan, and the heat is on. If the urge to check comes back, let it drift off like steam rising from the pan.
A small fish. In chapter sixty, ruling a great state is like cooking one: handle it lightly, or it falls apart. Today's word.
Your line: don't poke. Some things cook best when they're left alone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty as advice for anyone in charge of something fragile: set it up well, then hold back from constant meddling.

chat.says: Why would an old book compare running a country to cooking a fish?
options: A small fish falls apart if you keep stirring it. A country, too, needs light handling.
Fish was the country's main food, so rulers had to make sure everyone could cook it.
It means a ruler should cook for the people himself, to show he's one of them.

notes: Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 60 word for word.
The Heshang Gong commentary paraphrase (烹小鮮…不敢撓，恐其糜也) should be checked against the received commentary; the attribution to Heshang Gong is traditional, hence 'the one tradition credits to'.
The index hook's 'without too much poking' is the commentary's reading, not words in the chapter; the script says so.
